developments.title: Canada August payroll falls while weekly earnings growth accelerates
developments.facts: August payroll employment decreased 49,600 (-0.3%) after July -15,700 (-0.1%); employment rose 0.3% y/y. Losses spanned 10 of 20 sectors. Public administration -22,300 includes federal temporary Census staffing unwinding, so the full headline is not a private-demand collapse. Accommodation/food -6,800, information/culture -5,000, construction -4,500 and retail -4,400 add broader softness. Average weekly earnings rose 0.5% m/m to $1,355 and 3.7% y/y after 3.2%. Earnings mix includes composition, hours, wage and base effects; it is not a pure wage-rate measure. Weekly hours 33.4 were little changed m/m, +0.6% y/y. Vacancies 507,200 and vacancy rate 2.8% were little changed; unemployed per vacancy 2.9 unchanged. One lagged release package, not independent bullish/bearish votes. No unverified consensus surprise is asserted.

developments.title: BoC expected hike and cautious further-tightening path
developments.facts: The BoC raised 25 bp to 2.50% on October 28, as broadly anticipated. It revised the growth outlook upward, with 2027/2028 GDP around 2%, and projected more persistent inflation: annual-average 2027 inflation about 3%, one percentage point above July, returning to target around mid-2028. Core remains near 2%, CPI excluding gasoline 2.2%, unemployment around 6.5%, excess supply persists and tariffs weigh on Q4. Further increases are conditional and officials will proceed carefully. RBC's October 28 analysis retains a 100 bp total cycle (three further hikes after October) conditional on resilience, while acknowledging no current-data urgency, already-priced term yields and growth downside relative to BoC projections. Financial Post reports Bloomberg-attributed December hike odds falling to 55% after the decision from 100% Tuesday; Canadian Press separately attributes 43% to LSEG Wednesday afternoon. These provider/time snapshots are not interchangeable or a directly refreshed curve. CIBC/Desjardins favour another hike in January and 2.75% peak, illustrating forecast disagreement. Stronger growth/income and a possible longer cycle are support; the reported negative near-term path repricing is material opposition to a current strengthening claim.
